video_title: The Next Michael Burry | Animal Spirits 480
gist: Ben Carlson and Michael Batnick argue that the AI capex and debt boom — roughly $450-600bn of AI-related borrowing in 2026 and planned capex near 3% of GDP through 2029 — is now the dominant multi-year market story, and that the race to be the next Michael Burry who calls its top is a losing game. They plant a flag as 'team middle,' rejecting both the 10% GDP growth and the biggest-crash-in-history endings, and support it with the 2026 software round trip (IGV down ~40% and back within 7% of highs), broadening earnings outside the Mag 7, a record-low S&P dividend yield, an asset-manager M&A wave, benign-looking bond yields, and consumer and BNPL data that contradict negative sentiment surveys.

themes.theme: AI capex scale and the debt-funded buildout

insights.claim: AI companies' debt issuance has gone from roughly $27 billion last year to nearly $450 billion by mid-August, on pace for about $600 billion in 2026 — more than the combined budgets of the Departments of Justice, Transportation and Education.
insights.speaker: host (citing Robin Wigglesworth's New York Times op-ed)
insights.so_what: The AI trade is now a credit story as much as an equity story; watch AI-linked issuance and corporate spreads as the transmission channel if sentiment turns.
insights.quote: AI companies tap debt for $27 billion last year. Okay. By mid August, it's already close to$450 billion.

insights.claim: Planned AI capital expenditures are set to run at roughly 3% of GDP from 2027 to 2029, close to a trillion dollars a year on back-of-the-envelope math — a scale with no historical precedent.
insights.speaker: host (citing Robin Wigglesworth)
insights.so_what: Capex at 3% of GDP makes AI spending a macro variable: growth, industrial activity and rates all become AI-dependent, not just tech earnings.
insights.quote: Future capital expenditures planned to account for roughly 3% of GDP from 2027 to 2029.

insights.claim: Because AI capex is so large, the hosts argue the spending itself props up growth — huge numbers do not automatically imply a crash, they imply an economy that cannot easily slow while the money is being spent.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Frames AI capex as a near-term growth support rather than only a bubble marker; the bear case requires the spending to stop first, so capex guidance is the leading indicator.
insights.quote: If they keep spending this much money, there's no way the economy is going to stop and slow down.

insights.claim: Absent a collapse in AI capex, the hosts see a higher probability that the US avoids a recession for the rest of the decade than that it has one.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A no-recession base case argues for staying long cyclicals and credit, with the AI capex cycle rather than the labor market as the thing to monitor for a regime break.
insights.quote: if AI doesn't sync us, it's a higher probability event that we don't have a recession the rest of this decade than we do

insights.claim: Annualized token sales for the two leading AI labs alone are reported at more than $100 billion, up over 500% from a year ago, according to the Fed chair's Jackson Hole prepared remarks.
insights.speaker: host (reading Kevin Warsh's prepared remarks)
insights.so_what: Gives a revenue-side counterweight to the 'circular spending' critique: inference revenue is compounding fast enough that the Fed now treats AI as a factor of production.
insights.quote: Reports put annualized token sales for the two leading labs alone at more than 100 billion, an increase of 500 plus% from a year ago.

themes.theme: Calling the AI top versus team middle

insights.claim: The hosts argue the AI-bubble debate has spawned commentators competing to be the person who 'calls it' — modeled on Michael Burry and Steve Eisman — and that this incentive makes them move goalposts rather than update their views.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Discount forecasts from anyone whose brand depends on the crash arriving; check whether their thesis has been restated rather than falsified.
insights.quote: It's like I'll move the goalpost across the field if I have to.

insights.claim: Ed Zitron's rapid rise as an AI bear illustrates that in an attention economy, confident, fast, number-citing certainty builds an audience faster than accurate uncertainty does.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A signal-quality filter: rising audience share for a macro voice is evidence of confident delivery, not of forecast accuracy.
insights.quote: people seek certainty. And when you speak with confidence and you speak fast and you speak with numbers and you site sources, you build an audience.

insights.claim: Every bubble box — debt, circular deals, a weak productivity payoff, unchanged jobs data — has already been checked for years, and commentators have called the market long in the tooth since 2018, so hindsight obviousness is not evidence of foresight.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Bubble checklists have had near-zero timing value for the better part of a decade; treat them as risk-awareness inputs, not sell signals.
insights.quote: whatever outcome happens will be obvious as always

insights.claim: The hosts explicitly position themselves as 'team middle' on AI, arguing investors wrongly assume the ending must be extreme — either 10% GDP growth from productivity or the biggest crash in history.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: A muddle-through outcome is the least-positioned scenario; barbell hedges bought for a crash-or-boom resolution can bleed for years.
insights.quote: Ben, we're team middle. We're team middle, right?

insights.claim: Torsten Slok's framing is that rates fall either way — if AI succeeds it is massively deflationary, and if AI fails the Nasdaq drops 50% and money rotates into bonds — making him structurally bullish on duration.
insights.speaker: host (citing Torsten Slok)
insights.so_what: A rare AI-outcome-agnostic trade: long duration pays in both the productivity-boom and the bust branch, which is why bonds may be the cleanest AI hedge.
insights.quote: if AI succeeds, rates will be lower. If AI fails, rates will be lower

insights.claim: The hosts expect an AI bear market eventually but suggest it could end in a V-shaped bottom, an outcome that would satisfy neither the extreme bulls nor the extreme bears, partly because investors were conditioned by the dot-com and financial-crisis twin peaks to expect dramatic endings.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Plan the drawdown response in advance: a fast round trip punishes investors who de-risk into the low and wait for confirmation.
insights.quote: we had twin peaks and that that like scarred a generation of investors

themes.theme: Software's 2026 round trip as the AI playbook

insights.claim: Software stocks have almost fully round-tripped: IGV fell roughly 40% from its highs with individual names down 50-60%, and is now within 7% of all-time highs after rallying about 40% off the lows.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: The 'AI kills software' narrative was fully priced and then unwound within months — a template for how fast AI-disruption discounts can reverse in other sectors.
insights.quote: It's now less than 7% from the highs.

insights.claim: The software drawdown and recovery was a whipsaw rather than a clean V — a slow fall, a crash, a rebound, new lows, a 30%-plus ETF rally in weeks, then another quick crash before new recent highs — which made trading the disruption brutal even for someone positioned in it.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Path dependency matters more than the endpoint: even a correct disruption thesis was nearly untradeable, favoring position sizing over timing.
insights.quote: a monster run from, let's use the ETF for example, IGV, from 75 to a buckle five, so a 30% rally or more in a couple of weeks, and then another quick crash before rebounding to new highs

insights.claim: The hosts predict AI adoption will produce a decade of corporate overreaction cycles — companies laying off staff, regretting it, then rehiring — rather than a one-way displacement of workers.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Expect noisy headcount and margin data; single-quarter AI-driven layoff or rehiring announcements are weak evidence for a structural trend.
insights.quote: Companies are going to lay off a bunch of employees and go, "Oh crap, why did we do that?"

insights.claim: The lesson the hosts draw from software's round trip is that picking winners and losers actively through mega disruption is extremely difficult because consensus flips so quickly.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Argues for broad or index exposure to a disruption theme instead of concentrated single-name bets on who gets disrupted.
insights.quote: It's really hard to invest actively through mega disruption.

insights.claim: Rich Bernstein's screen of ACWI companies with consensus EPS growth estimates above 25% turns up roughly 200 stocks worldwide, of which only one is a Mag 7 company and many are foreign developed and emerging-market names.
insights.speaker: host (citing Rich Bernstein)
insights.so_what: Concrete support for taking growth exposure outside US mega-cap tech; the highest projected earnings growth is largely non-US and non-Mag 7.

insights.claim: Bernstein's view is that the market can rotate away from the momentum-driven AI and technology theme without a bear market, and that this rotation has been 2026's story so far.
insights.speaker: host (citing Rich Bernstein)
insights.so_what: The bearish AI case does not require an index drawdown — leadership change alone can hurt concentrated momentum portfolios while the index holds up.
insights.quote: Investors scoffed at our suggestion that the stock market could rotate away from the momentum driven AI and technology theme without a bare market. However, that has indeed been 2026's story so far.

insights.claim: Net margins for the S&P 500 excluding the Mag 7 — the '493' — have expanded to 13.6% from under 12% in 2024 and below 11% in Q4 2023, with projections near 15% by Q4 2027.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Margin expansion outside the AI capex spenders is the cleanest test of whether AI is a real productivity story rather than circular, debt-fueled revenue.

insights.claim: The hosts argue anyone who genuinely believes the AI productivity thesis must also be bullish the 493 non-Mag 7 companies, since those are the firms whose margins the technology is supposed to lift.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A consistency test for AI bulls, and a way to express the thesis with less concentration risk than owning the capex spenders.
insights.quote: if you think the technology for AI is going to do what the people say it's going to do, you have to be bullish on these other stocks on the 493

themes.theme: Bull-market plumbing: M&A, dividends, leverage rules

insights.claim: A burst of wealth- and asset-management M&A — Vanguard buying Altruist for $4-5 billion, T. Rowe Price acquiring FM Investments, Goldman Sachs buying both NEOS and Innovator, and Victory Capital acquiring First Eagle for $7 billion — is classic bull-market consolidation behavior.
insights.speaker: host (citing James Seyffart of Bloomberg)
insights.so_what: Deal flow in custodians and asset managers is a sentiment marker and tightens the competitive set for independent ETF issuers and RIA platforms.
insights.quote: This is all total bull market behavior. Asset managers getting acquired, custodians, right? Building scale.

insights.claim: The hosts defend the asset-management deal prices as rational on fundamentals — high margins plus a built-in growth kicker from rising markets — while conceding the entire case assumes markets keep going up.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Acquirer multiples in asset management are effectively a levered bet on market levels; a flat-to-down market would reprice these deals sharply.
insights.quote: if you think about the built-in growth rate underlying these businesses and the margins they have, then all of these deals probably make sense

insights.claim: The S&P 500 dividend yield has fallen to 98 basis points, believed to be the lowest in history, which the hosts attribute to non-dividend-paying tech companies making up roughly 40% of the index rather than to broad market excess.
insights.speaker: host (citing Tadas Viskanta and Bespoke)
insights.so_what: Treat the record-low dividend yield as a composition artifact, not a valuation signal — the historical yield comparison is broken by index concentration.
insights.quote: This is, I believe, the lowest level in history.

insights.claim: Turnover in South Korean single-stock leveraged ETFs tied to Samsung and SK Hynix collapsed from a peak near $50 billion to roughly zero within a week after regulators required a five-day simulated-trading course run on a Windows-only PC program.
insights.speaker: host (citing Bloomberg)
insights.so_what: A live experiment showing that friction, not education, kills speculative volume — relevant to any jurisdiction weighing leveraged single-stock product rules.
insights.quote: Investors must download a Windows only program on PCs and spend at least an hour a day learning the ropes and the risks of leverage trading with virtual cash.

insights.claim: The hosts contrast South Korea's ability to legislate away speculative behavior with the US, where they argue comparable restrictions on retail leverage would be politically impossible.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: US retail speculation is a structurally durable source of flow because the regulatory brake other markets use is unavailable here.
insights.quote: when bad behavior happens, all these other countries can kind of wave a magic wand and just like put rules on it and it goes away. But we would we would never do this in a million years here.

insights.claim: Matthew Klein of The Overshoot argues rising bond yields are benign because incomes and spending are rising about 7% a year in dollar terms, making a 10-year Treasury below 5% in those conditions the opposite of a disorderly market.
insights.speaker: host (citing Matthew Klein, The Overshoot)
insights.so_what: Reframes the yield backup as confirmation of nominal growth rather than a fiscal crisis signal — bearish for duration but not for risk assets.
insights.quote: today's rates are obviously too high only if inflation and growth are both poised to slow sharply here

insights.claim: Real GDP per American rose less between 2007 and 2019 than it did between 1929 and 1941, which the hosts use to argue that nostalgia for the low-rate 2010s ignores how weak that decade's growth actually was.
insights.speaker: host (citing Matthew Klein)
insights.so_what: Supports preferring the higher-growth, higher-inflation, higher-rate 2020s regime over a return to secular stagnation — a very different allocation baseline.
insights.quote: Real GDP per American rose less between 2007 and 2019 than it did between 1929 and 1941.

insights.claim: The hosts contend investors are unsettled by the direction of interest rates rather than the level, which is why a historically normal yield still feels alarming.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Explains why sentiment and rate levels diverge; positioning reacts to the slope of yields, not their absolute value.
insights.quote: I think people are maybe rightly concerned more about the direction than the level

insights.claim: The hosts argue the bond market is correctly taking its cue from the macroeconomy — tax cuts, elevated government spending and deficits mean yields should be higher, not that the market is broken.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Argues against betting on a rapid yield collapse absent a growth shock; the fiscal impulse is the dominant driver of the term structure.
insights.quote: We had all these tax cuts. We have all this government spending. We have deficits. Of course, rates should be higher.

insights.claim: The new Fed chair used his Jackson Hole remarks to argue against publishing forecasts that illustrate the Fed's reaction function, citing 2021 forward guidance as an example of guidance slowing the policy response to high inflation.
insights.speaker: host (reading Kevin Warsh)
insights.so_what: If the Fed de-emphasizes forecasts and forward guidance, rate volatility should shift toward data releases and away from Fed communications.
insights.quote: Providing forecast to illustrate the Fed's reaction function works better in theory than in practice, better in the lab than in the field.

insights.claim: Retail and fintech CEOs on recent earnings calls — Urban Outfitters, Gap and Affirm's Max Levchin — all described the consumer as solid, with Urban Outfitters citing real job stability and rising take-home incomes.
insights.speaker: host (quoting earnings-call transcripts)
insights.so_what: Company-level commentary is running well ahead of sentiment surveys; favor hard spending data over confidence readings for consumer-exposed positioning.
insights.quote: based on what we see across our businesses every day, the economy and the customers remain in very solid shape. Job stability is real.

insights.claim: The hosts argue consumer surveys are constructed to produce negative results, citing a Bloomberg-reported finding that three-quarters of US adults feel guilty spending on things that bring them joy.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A standing reason to downweight soft sentiment data in macro models when it conflicts with spending and earnings evidence.
insights.quote: Survey results are negative on purpose.

insights.claim: Affirm's 30-day delinquencies on monthly installment loans excluding Peloton remain very low at about 2.5%, and the stock now carries a roughly $24 billion market cap, well below its 2021 meme-stock peak.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: BNPL credit performance is a real-time read on subprime-adjacent consumer health, and it is not flashing stress.

insights.claim: The hosts' verdict on the buy-now-pay-later debate is that skeptics were right about the valuations — Affirm and Klarna both crashed from 2021 peaks, with Klarna marked around $40 billion privately before falling to roughly $6 billion — but wrong that BNPL growth signaled a tapped-out consumer.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A reusable distinction: an asset can be badly mispriced without the macro signal bears attached to it being correct — separate the valuation call from the economic call.
insights.quote: where people were wrong were it was a sign that the consumer is totally tapped out

insights.claim: Consumers took roughly four years to accept post-pandemic price levels, illustrated by the host paying $13 for a Chipotle bowl without blinking and concluding it is simply what lunch costs now.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Price-level anger fades on a multi-year lag even while inflation grievance polling stays elevated — supportive for pricing power at scaled restaurant brands.
insights.quote: I have now fully adjusted to a $13 Chipotle bowl.

insights.claim: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate is back near 6.8% and approaching 7%, and the mortgage-Treasury spread has compressed so much that at the spread of a few years ago the rate would be closer to 8%.
insights.speaker: host (citing Logan Mohtashami)
insights.so_what: Spread compression has already delivered a hidden chunk of mortgage relief; further affordability improvement now requires Treasury yields to fall.
insights.quote: we're we're getting very close to 7% mortgage rates again, which is pretty insane to think about

insights.claim: The hosts note inflation is running high while roughly 20% of the economy — housing — is already in recession, and ask what happens to inflation if housing activity rebounds when rates eventually fall.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A housing recovery could be inflationary rather than disinflationary, complicating the assumption that rate cuts are unambiguously good for bonds.
insights.quote: It's interesting to think about the fact of how high inflation already is while 20% of the economy is in a recession.

insights.claim: Redfin data shows homeownership by generation at roughly 80% for baby boomers, 73% for Gen X, 55% for millennials and under 30% for Gen Z — but Gen Z is tracking right where millennials were at the same age.
insights.speaker: host (citing a Redfin report)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'young people will never own homes' narrative and argues against permanently writing down first-time-buyer demand in housing forecasts.

insights.claim: The hosts predict a large Gen Z housing demand surge in the 2030s as baby boomers begin dying in waves and transfer wealth, mirroring how the 2010s 'millennials will never buy a home' narrative was proven wrong.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Supports a long-horizon bullish view on housing demand and homebuilders despite current affordability stress.
insights.quote: In the 2030s, there's going to be a massive come up for Gen Z buying houses.

insights.claim: Census data covering hundreds of thousands of firms, highlighted by Alex Tabarrok at Marginal Revolution, shows 2.3% of firms increased employment because of AI, about 2% decreased it, and 96% reported no change, with similar answers across firm sizes.
insights.speaker: host (citing Alex Tabarrok, Marginal Revolution)
insights.so_what: The measurable labor-market impact of AI is still a rounding error, which argues against trading the AI-displacement thesis in labor-sensitive sectors today.
insights.quote: There's it's basically a rounding error, the impact AI has had on jobs.

insights.claim: The hosts argue AI-disruption bears who have been pounding the table without the disruption materializing owe themselves the question of whether they are simply wrong, instead of defaulting to 'it's still early.'
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A falsifiability test to apply to any long-running thesis: define what evidence would change the view before that evidence arrives.
insights.quote: If you've been pounding the table for the disruption from this and it hasn't happened, you have to have an open mind that what if I'm wrong?

insights.claim: Data-center siting is becoming a local political problem, illustrated by an AWS facility in Ashburn, Virginia built directly beside residential neighborhoods, with the hosts arguing power and water infrastructure — not land availability — forces the buildout near populated areas.
insights.speaker: host (citing a Bloomberg article)
insights.so_what: Grid and water constraints plus local opposition are the binding limits on AI capex deployment, making power infrastructure the choke point to watch.

insights.claim: Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness fund pitch cited hedge fund managers who got the thesis right but blew up on risk management, with rules one and two being 'don't blow up' — a line the host notes has not aged well.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick (recounting the Dwarkesh Patel podcast)
insights.so_what: In a concentrated AI-thesis fund, being right on direction is not sufficient — position sizing and drawdown control determine survival.
insights.quote: he said rule number one and number two don't blow up which obviously didn't age age great
